questions.question: What is the Masked Language Modeling (MLM) pre-training objective?
options: Predict the next token given all previous tokens
Randomly mask 15% of tokens and predict the original tokens from context in both directions
Classify the sentiment of each sentence
Generate a paraphrase of the input
questions.explanation: MLM masks ~15% of input tokens (replaced with [MASK], a random token, or kept unchanged) and trains the model to predict the original tokens using both left and right context. This bidirectional context makes BERT great for understanding tasks.

questions.question: What does the [CLS] token in BERT represent?
options: The classifier for next-sentence prediction
A special token prepended to every input whose final hidden state is used as the sequence-level representation
The end-of-sequence marker
A masking placeholder
questions.explanation: [CLS] is prepended to every input. After the encoder runs, the [CLS] hidden state aggregates information from the entire sequence through attention and is used as the input to classification heads for downstream tasks.

questions.question: Why can't BERT be used directly for text generation?
options: It doesn't have enough parameters
It uses bidirectional attention — it sees the full sequence at once, so it can't generate autoregressively
It doesn't have a decoder
It only supports English
questions.explanation: BERT's bidirectional self-attention means every token attends to all other tokens simultaneously. Generation requires predicting the next token without seeing future tokens — a constraint that requires causal (left-to-right) attention, not bidirectional attention.

questions.question: What is the Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task in BERT, and why was it removed in RoBERTa?
options: NSP predicts missing words; RoBERTa found it too slow
NSP predicts whether two sentences are consecutive; RoBERTa found it was either too easy or harmful to MLM performance
NSP classifies sentence types; RoBERTa replaced it with paragraph prediction
NSP was a translation task
questions.explanation: NSP trains BERT to predict whether sentence B follows sentence A. RoBERTa's ablation found NSP was either trivially solved or hurt performance, so they removed it and trained longer with more data and larger batches — significantly outperforming BERT.

questions.question: What is the typical fine-tuning approach for BERT on a classification task?
options: Freeze all layers, train only the embedding layer
Add a linear classifier on the [CLS] token output and fine-tune all parameters end-to-end
Replace BERT's final layer with a new transformer block
Train the entire model from scratch on the downstream task
questions.explanation: For classification, add a linear head on the [CLS] token output. Fine-tune all BERT weights jointly with the classifier, using a small learning rate (2-5e-5). The pre-trained weights give a strong initialization that converges in just a few epochs.
